blocks.text: Most probability questions people actually care about are not about the full space of possibilities, they are about a narrower situation that has already partly resolved. What is the chance it rains given the sky is already cloudy, what is the chance an email is spam given it contains the word free, what is the chance a patient has a disease given a test came back positive. Conditional probability is the formal tool for updating a probability once new information restricts the space of outcomes still on the table.

blocks.alt: Conditioning on an event shrinks the sample space down to the part where that event is true
blocks.caption: Conditioning restricts attention to the world where B already happened

blocks.text: 1. What Conditional Probability Means

Conditional probability, written P(A given B) or P(A|B), is the probability that event A happens given that event B is already known to have happened. It answers a narrower question than the plain probability P(A), because it only looks inside the world where B is true, ignoring everything that happens when B does not hold.

The formal definition is P(A|B) equals P(A and B) divided by P(B), defined only when P(B) is greater than zero. The numerator is the joint probability that both events happen, and the denominator rescales that joint probability so it is measured against the smaller world of B rather than against the entire original sample space.

code.content:
p_a_and_b = 0.20   # P(cold and rain)
p_b = 0.30         # P(rain)
p_a_given_b = p_a_and_b / p_b
print(round(p_a_given_b, 3))   # 0.667

blocks.text: The vertical bar in P(A|B) is read out loud as given, so P(A|B) is spoken as the probability of A given B, and it is worth remembering the bar is not division, the actual division only appears once the formula is written out in full as P(A and B) over P(B).
2. Reading Conditional Probability from a Table

A joint probability table makes conditional probability easy to compute directly. To find P(A given B), take the cell or cells corresponding to A and B together, and divide by the total probability in the row or column corresponding to B alone, which is exactly the marginal probability of B.

To find P(Cold given Rain), take the Cold and Rain cell, 0.20, and divide by the Rain column total, 0.20 plus 0.10, which is 0.30. That gives P(Cold given Rain) equals 0.667, meaning that whenever it is raining, it turns out cold about two thirds of the time.

code.content:
import numpy as np
joint = np.array([[0.20, 0.15],
                   [0.10, 0.55]])
p_rain = joint[:, 0].sum()          # 0.30, marginal of rain
p_cold_given_rain = joint[0, 0] / p_rain
print(round(p_cold_given_rain, 3))   # 0.667

blocks.text: The same table also gives P(Rain given Cold) by reading down the Cold row instead of across the Rain column, 0.20 divided by the Cold row total of 0.35, which comes out to 0.571, a different number from P(Cold given Rain) computed above, a first concrete illustration of the asymmetry covered in full in section 7 below.
3. The Multiplication Rule, Revisited

The multiplication rule from the probability rules lesson states that P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B) only when A and B are independent. The general version, which holds for every pair of events regardless of independence, is P(A and B) equals P(A given B) times P(B), or equivalently P(B given A) times P(A). Conditional probability is what makes the general multiplication rule work.

Rearranging the conditional probability definition gives exactly this general multiplication rule, since multiplying both sides of P(A|B) equals P(A and B) over P(B) by P(B) leaves P(A and B) equals P(A|B) times P(B). Independence is simply the special case where conditioning on B changes nothing, so P(A|B) collapses down to plain P(A), covered in full in the independence lesson elsewhere in this module.

code.content:
p_b = 0.30
p_a_given_b = 0.667
p_a_and_b = p_a_given_b * p_b
print(round(p_a_and_b, 2))   # 0.20, matches the joint table cell

blocks.text: Because P(A and B) is symmetric, meaning P(A and B) always equals P(B and A), the two forms of the general multiplication rule must agree, so P(A given B) times P(B) always equals P(B given A) times P(A), a small identity that turns out to be exactly the equation Bayes theorem is built from.
4. Conditioning Narrows the Sample Space

A useful mental picture of conditional probability is a Venn diagram where conditioning on B means throwing away everything outside the B circle and treating the remaining B circle as the entire new universe. P(A given B) is then just the fraction of that new, smaller universe that is also covered by A.

blocks.alt: Conditioning on B keeps only the part of the diagram inside the B circle
blocks.caption: P(A given B) is the overlap region measured as a fraction of the whole B circle, not the whole diagram

blocks.text: A relative frequency reading of the same picture says the same thing without any circles, imagine repeating an experiment many times and throwing away every trial where B did not happen, P(A given B) is then just the fraction of the surviving, B only trials where A also happened.
5. Conditional Probability in Code

Computing a conditional probability in code almost always reduces to two lookups and one division, the joint probability of both events and the marginal probability of the condition. The same pattern extends cleanly from a hand built table to real data by simply counting rows instead of reading table cells.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.DataFrame({
    "weather": ["rain", "rain", "no_rain", "no_rain", "rain"],
    "temp": ["cold", "warm", "cold", "warm", "cold"],
})
p_b = (data["weather"] == "rain").mean()
p_a_and_b = ((data["weather"] == "rain") & (data["temp"] == "cold")).mean()
p_a_given_b = p_a_and_b / p_b
print(round(p_a_given_b, 3))

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Out of five logged days, three are rainy and two of those three rainy days are also cold. So P(cold and rain) equals 2/5, or 0.40, and P(rain) equals 3/5, or 0.60. Dividing gives P(cold given rain) equals 0.667, exactly matching the count based intuition that two out of three rainy days were cold.

code.content:
from scipy.stats import bernoulli
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
weather = bernoulli.rvs(0.30, size=100000, random_state=rng)          # 1 = rain
temp = np.where(weather == 1, bernoulli.rvs(0.667, size=100000, random_state=rng), bernoulli.rvs(0.176, size=100000, random_state=rng))
estimated = temp[weather == 1].mean()
print(round(estimated, 3))   # close to 0.667, recovered empirically from simulated data

blocks.text: 6. The Complement Rule Inside a Condition

The complement rule from the probability rules lesson, P(not A) equals 1 minus P(A), carries over unchanged once everything is conditioned on the same event B. P(not A given B) equals 1 minus P(A given B), because within the restricted world of B, A and not A still cover every possibility and still cannot both happen.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: If P(late given rain) is 0.80 for a commute, then P(on time given rain) must be 1 minus 0.80, which is 0.20, since on any rainy day the commute is either late or on time, and those two outcomes still exhaust every possibility once rain is fixed as the condition.

blocks.text: 7. Why P(A|B) Does Not Equal P(B|A)

One of the most common mistakes with conditional probability is silently swapping the order, treating P(A given B) as if it were the same number as P(B given A). They are almost never equal, and confusing the two is sometimes called the prosecutors fallacy because of how badly it can distort legal and medical reasoning.

A quick sanity check makes the asymmetry obvious, P(rain given clouds) is fairly high since clouds usually precede rain, but P(clouds given rain) is close to certain since it essentially always is cloudy while it rains, two very different numbers describing the same pair of events in opposite directions. Untangling exactly how the two directions relate to each other is the whole subject of the bayes theorem lesson that follows this one.

code.content:
p_rain_given_clouds = 0.40
p_clouds_given_rain = 0.95
print(p_rain_given_clouds == p_clouds_given_rain)   # False, order genuinely matters

blocks.text: The same asymmetry is exactly why a medical test result is so easy to misread, P(positive test given disease) can be very high, close to 99 percent for a good test, while P(disease given positive test) can still be quite low if the disease itself is rare to begin with, a full worked version of this exact scenario opens the bayes theorem lesson that follows.
8. Conditional Probability and Independence

Two events A and B are defined to be independent precisely when conditioning on B does not move the probability of A at all, formally P(A given B) equals plain P(A). Whenever this holds, the general multiplication rule collapses back down to the simple form P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B) from the probability rules lesson.

This gives a direct test for independence using nothing but conditional probability, compute P(A given B) and compare it to P(A). If they match, B carries no information about A. If they differ, even slightly, A and B are dependent, and the independence lesson elsewhere in this module works through this test in much greater depth.

code.content:
p_cold = 0.35
p_cold_given_rain = 0.667
print(p_cold == p_cold_given_rain)   # False, so cold and rain are dependent

import numpy as np
joint = np.array([[0.30, 0.25],
                   [0.20, 0.25]])   # rows: car / no car, cols: city / not city
p_car = joint[0, :].sum()
p_car_given_city = joint[0, 0] / joint[:, 0].sum()
print(round(p_car, 3), round(p_car_given_city, 3))   # different numbers, so dependent

blocks.text: 9. Chaining Multiple Conditions

Conditional probability is not limited to conditioning on a single event, P(A given B and C) is a perfectly well formed conditional probability meaning the probability of A once both B and C are known to hold, computed the same way by restricting the sample space to where B and C are both true and measuring A within that space.

Repeatedly applying the general multiplication rule gives the chain rule of probability, P(A and B and C) equals P(A) times P(B given A) times P(C given A and B), a pattern that extends to any number of events and underlies how many sequential models, including language models, factor a joint probability into a product of conditional steps.

code.content:
p_a = 0.5
p_b_given_a = 0.4
p_c_given_a_and_b = 0.7
p_all_three = p_a * p_b_given_a * p_c_given_a_and_b
print(round(p_all_three, 3))   # 0.14

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Drawing three cards in a row without replacement from a shuffled deck, P(first is a heart) is 13 over 52, P(second is a heart given first was a heart) is 12 over 51, and P(third is a heart given the first two were hearts) is 11 over 50, so the chain rule multiplies all three fractions together to get the probability of drawing three hearts in a row.

blocks.text: 10. Conditional Probability in Naive Bayes Classifiers

Naive Bayes classifiers are built almost entirely out of conditional probability. To classify an email as spam or not spam, the model estimates P(spam given the words in the email), and the whole training process is really just estimating conditional probabilities like P(the word free appears given the email is spam) from labeled examples.

The word naive refers to a simplifying assumption made about those conditional probabilities, that each word contributes independently once the class label is known, which turns an otherwise intractable joint conditional probability into a simple product of single word conditional probabilities that is cheap to compute.
10.1 The Conditional Independence Assumption

Formally, naive Bayes assumes P(word one and word two given spam) equals P(word one given spam) times P(word two given spam), which is exactly the independence condition from section 8 above, but applied conditionally on the class label rather than unconditionally. This is called conditional independence, and the independence lesson later in this module returns to the distinction between plain independence and conditional independence in more depth.

code.content:
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[3, 0], [0, 2], [2, 0], [0, 3]])   # word counts: [free, meeting]
y = np.array(["spam", "not_spam", "spam", "not_spam"])
model = MultinomialNB()
model.fit(X, y)
print(model.predict_proba([[2, 0]]))   # P(class given word counts) for a new email

blocks.text: 11. Conditional Probability in Language Models

A language model predicting the next word is, under the hood, computing a conditional probability, P(next token given every token that came before it). Generating a full sentence one token at a time is really sampling from a long chain of these conditional probabilities, exactly the chain rule structure introduced in section 9 above.

This is why the same context can push a model toward wildly different next tokens, the conditional probability distribution over the vocabulary genuinely changes as the conditioning context changes, which is the entire mechanism that lets a language model produce context appropriate text rather than the same fixed output every time.

code.content:
# Conceptually, a language model scores the next token as a conditional probability
# P(token_t | token_1, token_2, ..., token_{t-1})
context = ["the", "sky", "is"]
# a trained model would return something like:
next_token_probs = {"blue": 0.62, "clear": 0.11, "falling": 0.01}
print(max(next_token_probs, key=next_token_probs.get))   # "blue"

blocks.text: The sampling temperature setting exposed by many language model APIs directly reshapes this conditional distribution before a token is drawn, a lower temperature sharpens the distribution toward whichever token already has the highest conditional probability, while a higher temperature flattens it out and gives lower probability tokens a more realistic chance of being chosen.
12. Conditional Probability in AI Practice More Broadly

items: Recommendation systems estimate P(click given user features and item features), a conditional probability learned from historical interaction logs rather than looked up from a hand built table.
Anomaly detection systems often flag a data point when P(observed value given the normal operating condition) is very low, exactly the conditional probability framing used throughout this lesson.

Medical and fraud detection models report scores that are, explicitly or implicitly, conditional probabilities like P(fraud given transaction features), which the bayes theorem lesson shows how to relate back to the reverse conditional probability P(features given fraud) that is often easier to estimate from data.

blocks.text: Whenever a machine learning model outputs something described as a score or a confidence given some input, it is almost always reporting a conditional probability, whether or not the word conditional ever appears in the documentation.

Model evaluation metrics themselves often hide a conditional probability inside their definition, precision is P(actually positive given predicted positive) and recall is P(predicted positive given actually positive), two conditional probabilities that condition in opposite directions and are frequently confused for exactly the reason section 7 above describes.
13. A Worked Example

A factory runs two machines, Machine A produces 60 percent of all parts and Machine B produces the remaining 40 percent. Of the parts from Machine A, 2 percent are defective, and of the parts from Machine B, 5 percent are defective. A part is picked at random and found to be defective. What fraction of all parts are both from Machine A and defective.

code.content:
p_a = 0.60          # P(Machine A)
p_defect_given_a = 0.02
p_a_and_defect = p_a * p_defect_given_a
print(round(p_a_and_defect, 4))   # 0.012, this is P(Machine A and defective)

blocks.text: That 0.012 is a joint probability, not yet the conditional probability of Machine A given the part is defective. Computing P(Machine A given defective) requires dividing by the total probability a part is defective at all, gathered from both machines together, which is exactly the setup the bayes theorem lesson picks up and finishes.

Notice the setup only gives conditional probabilities for defects within each machine separately, P(defective given Machine A) and P(defective given Machine B), the harder and more interesting question, the probability a defective part actually came from Machine A, requires combining both machines together and is picked up directly at the start of the bayes theorem lesson.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Swapping the order of conditioning, treating P(A given B) as interchangeable with P(B given A), the exact mistake covered in section 7 above.

Dividing by the wrong marginal, using P(A) in the denominator instead of P(B) when computing P(A given B), which produces a number that does not correspond to any well defined conditional probability.
Forgetting that P(A given B) is only defined when P(B) is greater than zero, and dividing by a marginal probability of exactly zero without checking for it first.
Assuming conditioning never changes anything, silently treating P(A given B) as equal to P(A) without actually checking, which quietly assumes independence that may not hold.

Confusing a conditional probability with a joint probability, reading P(A given B) as if it described the same fraction of the whole sample space as P(A and B), when it actually describes a fraction of just the B region.

blocks.text: Nearly every one of these mistakes traces back to the same root cause, treating conditional probability as a plain probability instead of remembering that it is always measured against a restricted sample space defined by whatever sits to the right of the given bar.
15. Practice: Compute a Conditional Probability

A survey of 200 people records whether each person owns a car and whether each person lives in a city, summarized in the joint probability table below. Compute P(owns a car given lives in a city) and compare it to the overall probability of owning a car.

code.content:
import numpy as np
joint = np.array([[0.30, 0.25],
                   [0.20, 0.25]])
p_city = joint[:, 0].sum()
p_car_and_city = joint[0, 0]
p_car_given_city = p_car_and_city / p_city
p_car_marginal = joint[0, :].sum()
print(round(p_car_given_city, 3), round(p_car_marginal, 3))

blocks.text: Compare the computed P(owns a car given lives in a city) against the plain marginal P(owns a car). A noticeable gap between the two numbers is itself evidence that city living and car ownership are not independent, exactly the kind of check the independence lesson formalizes.

As a further check, also compute P(lives in a city given owns a car) from the same table, and confirm it is a different number from P(owns a car given lives in a city), a direct hands on rehearsal of the asymmetry from section 7.
Key Takeaway

Conditional probability rescales the sample space down to whatever has already been conditioned on, and P(A given B) equals P(A and B) divided by P(B) is the single formula underlying every use of it, from reading a joint table by hand to a naive Bayes classifier scoring an email or a language model choosing its next token.

The direction of conditioning always matters, P(A given B) and P(B given A) are generally different numbers describing different questions, and untangling exactly how those two directions relate to each other, using the prior probability of each event, is precisely the subject the bayes theorem lesson takes up next.
